Catholic life
Westminster Cathedral Choir School is a school of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Westminster.
You can download the Archdiocese’s most recent inspection report here.
Like Gerard Manley Hopkins we believe that the Catholic faith has ‘only to be known, to be loved’, and we aim to teach and share it with joy, gentleness and fidelity.
The School places the transmission of the Catholic faith as its foremost aim, in the context of an outstanding, classical and demanding academic education for boys, and an enriching extra-curricular life. The School’s aims are:
We also follow the Golden Rule: Do to others that you would have them do to you (Matthew 7:12).
Boys meet every morning to pray and sing hymns in either a whole-School, form or house assembly. Each form takes it in turn to prepare an assembly about their form saint, or an important aspect of the liturgical year.
Pre-Prep boys (Reception – Year 3) say the prayer of St Francis Assisi daily; Prep boys (Years 4 – 8) say different prayers, including the prayer of St Ignatius.
We encourage boys to learn the prayers with the help of their parents, and each form has a prayer monitor to keep boys’ practice regular and faithful.
Lord, make me an instrument of your peace: where there is hatred, let me sow love; where there is injury, pardon; where there is doubt, faith; where there is despair, hope; where there is darkness, light; where there is sadness, joy.
O divine Master, grant that I may not so much seek to be consoled as to console, to be understood as to understand, to be loved as to love. For it is in giving that we receive; it is in pardoning that we are pardoned; and it is in dying that we are born to eternal life.
Dearest Jesus, teach me to be generous; teach me to love and serve you as you deserve: to give and not to count the cost; to fight and not to heed the wounds; to toil and not to seek for rest; to labour and to look for no reward, save that of knowing that I do your Holy Will. Through Christ Our Lord.
To offer all boys outstanding musical opportunities
To offer all boys enriching extra-curricular activities
Patrons
All boys offer prayers of intercession to our School’s patrons: Our Lady of Westminster and St Gregory the Great.
The late medieval statue of the virgin & child, Our Lady of Westminster, is at the entrance of the Lady Chapel in Westminster Cathedral where School Mass is celebrated every Tuesday.
St Gregory the Great was elected pope in 590: the first monk ever to hold the Petrine office. As a Choir School we have adopted Pope Gregory as our patron because he developed Gregorian chant – the plainsong sung every day in Westminster Cathedral.
We also encourage boys and staff to follow St Gregory’s example. He had a great love for the poor and preferred to be called ‘the servant of the servants of God’.
The Cathedral is at the heart of the School, both physically and spiritually. You can hear the choristers sing Mass every day except Saturdays during term time.
All boys in Year 3 – 8 attend School Mass in the Lady Chapel every Tuesday during term time. All parents are also invited to attend. Boys contribute to, and participate in, the Mass either by serving, reading or singing.
Altar servers also have the opportunity to serve at some of the Cathedral’s evening Masses and major feast days.
Boys in Year 3 and 4 are prepared for First Confession and First Holy Communion each year, if their parents wish, with weekly catechesis from Juliet Rodger and Emily Auger. Preparation begins after each Michaelmas half term; boys receive the sacraments in the Trinity (summer) term.
If your son would like receive instruction, please contact Robert O’Brien.
Email robrien@choirschool.com
Westminster Cathedral Choir School is a charity, and has a long and distinguished record of providing bursary support for choristers to attend the School. The School also shares the late Pope Francis’s commitment to serving the poor.
The School supports three designated charities each year: currently the Cardinal Hume Centre, Mary’s Meals and Eyehope. Boys learn that this is part of the School’s Catholic ethos, as well as their Christian obligation.
At Christmas the Gallery Choir sings for a number of charities, including Great Ormond St Hospital, and it raises funds for St Mary’s Cadogan Street, a church of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Westminster. Choristers sing in the wards of St Thomas’s Hospital in the days before Christmas.

Music
Music
Music
Music is both a curriculum subject and an extra-curricular activity at Westminster Cathedral Choir School.
Choristers are taught both by the Master of Music (in charge of the Cathedral Choir) and by the School’s Head of Music (in charge of School orchestras, ensembles and the organisation of instrumental lessons).
Every chorister receives the following formal musical tuition, every week, during term time.
Piano* (1 lesson) Singing* (1 lesson) Orchestral instrument (1 lesson)
*Piano and singing lessons are funded by the School; orchestral instrument lessons are charged to parents.
Day boys from Years 3 to 8 can have tuition in up to two instruments per week, from the following list:
Tuition in a musical instrument is optional for day boys.
Both choristers and day boys can join ensemble groups once they have reached the appropriate standard. These groups are selected by the Head of Music, but boys are encouraged to express interest if they have not been chosen. The following ensembles currently take place:
There are many opportunities for choristers and day boys to sing at WCCS.
The Gallery Choir is for senior boys, and sings at School Mass every Tuesday in the Cathedral, as well as in School concerts and external events. Entry is by audition only.
Recent highlights have also included performances at the Cadogan Hall and the unveiling of a portrait of Charles Dickens at the Philip Mould Gallery.
The Junior Choir consists of boys from Years 4 to 5 and performs at one School Mass each term and at School concerts during the year.
In addition to School and class assemblies, class music lessons and a weekly hymn practice, boys in the Pre-Prep have the chance to sing in the Reception & Year 1 choir or Year 2 & Year 3 choir, which rehearse once a week. Throughout the year there are other musical events, such as the School nativity (Reception), Christmas carol assembly (Year 1), School carol service (Year 3) and the House singing competition in the Lent term.
Class music lessons are part of the academic timetable. The curriculum includes a combination of historical, theoretical and practical music-making, and develops aural, compositional and singing skills in all year groups.

Head's welcome
Welcome to Westminster Cathedral Choir School (WCCS).
WCCS is an academically selective Catholic preparatory school for around 250 boys aged four to thirteen, from Reception to Year 8. Twenty-one boys board as choristers, joining in Year 4.
WCCS is a school for families who want an education that is intellectually serious, carefully taught and grounded in values.
A liberal academic education begins from a simple conviction: some knowledge matters because it is worth knowing. It does not justify itself by immediate usefulness or measurable outcomes. It justifies itself because it shapes judgement, enlarges understanding and endures.
A boy who studies history, for example, does not do so in order to become a historian. He learns how societies establish order, how authority claims legitimacy and how laws, customs and institutions grow or decay over time. He gains proportion, learning to judge the present in the light of the past rather than treating the moment as absolute.
A boy who studies demanding poetry does not do so in order to become a poet. He learns that language carries weight, that meaning depends on form and that attention sharpens truthfulness. He learns to recognise seriousness over noise and depth over display.
The same discipline governs mathematics and science. A boy who works through arithmetic, geometry or elementary physics does not do so to acquire a marketable skill. He learns how an argument unfolds, how conclusions depend on evidence and how reality resists wishful thinking. He discovers that accuracy matters and that truth does not bend to preference.
A liberal academic education stands apart from two modern temptations.
The first turns education into ideology. Lessons become vehicles for approved opinions or moral instruction. A liberal education refuses this role. It does not instruct boys what to think. It places knowledge before the mind and allows judgement to grow through understanding.
The second turns education into product. Screens, platforms and programmes promise efficiency, engagement and ease. Learning becomes delivery, knowledge becomes content and difficulty disappears. A liberal education resists this as well. It accepts effort, slowness and resistance because these are the conditions under which attention forms and judgement matures.
For this reason, the School insists on the basics. Secure arithmetic enables real mathematical problem solving. Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar enable boys to express ideas clearly and, in time, to write with elegance.
A liberal academic education does not seek to prescribe destinies; it seeks to multiply them.
Former pupils may become doctors, bankers or lawyers; they may become musicians, scientists or Jesuits. Their education does not choose their destinies. It forms the judgement of the person who chooses.
Music, sport and extra-curricular life form an essential part of education at Westminster Cathedral Choir School.
Choristers sing to a world-class standard and day boys participate fully in music-making. Coaches train teams carefully and competitively in football, rugby and cricket. Clubs and activities run with purpose, encouraging commitment, discipline and pride in improvement.
WCCS is a Catholic school in the fullest sense: intellectually serious, culturally rich and rooted in faith. The Catholic faith is taught with joy, gentleness and fidelity, trusting, as Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote, that it has ‘only to be known, to be loved’.
WCCS keeps screen use to an absolute minimum at every age.
This is a deliberate choice. Research consistently links excessive screen exposure between the ages of four and thirteen with weaker attention, reduced reading stamina, poorer memory, delayed language development and higher anxiety. Screens also crowd out what matters most in learning: concentration, reasoning and the ability to stay with difficulty rather than seek distraction.
Teaching therefore relies on books, handwriting, spoken discussion, mental calculation, memorisation and step-by-step problem solving. Technology appears where it genuinely helps — when preparing boys for competitive academic assessments, for example — but it never replaces thought or effort.
Nothing explains WCCS better than visiting it.
I hope you’ll come and see us.

Sports & clubs
Sports & clubs
Sports & clubs
The School is fortunate to have two large, secure, all-purpose playgrounds that boys from Reception to Year 8 use for imaginative play, football, nets practice and team tournaments of various kinds.
The School also uses the Battersea Park, Vincent Square playing fields, and the Queen Mother Sports Centre in Pimlico.
The main sports are football in the Michaelmas term, rugby in the Lent term and cricket in the Trinity term. Boys also take part in swimming, tennis, cross-country, judo, handball, athletics and fencing.
There is a busy fixture list, involving every boy in the School; a typical term will mean over sixty matches, as well as inter-house competitions. Qualified coaches work alongside members of the teaching staff.
School clubs take place after School, Monday to Friday, during term times. They vary termly according to interest and enthusiasm. Below is the clubs list for the Michaelmas term 2026.

Governors
David Heminway read Theology at King's College, London and a PGCE at the University of Cambridge. He held a number of senior academic and pastoral posts at the City of London School and for many years served on the School's Senior Management Team as Director of Admissions. David also oversaw the relationship between City and the Chapel Royal and the Temple Church, whose choristers were pupils at the School.
He retired in December 2014 but maintains his connection with the independent schools admissions world through consultancy work.
David is a communicant Anglican and worships at a traditionalist Anglo Catholic church, where he has helped extensively with the life of the parish, having been a long-standing trustee and PCC Secretary. He enjoys reading, music, cooking, the company of friends, visiting European cities, and travelling further afield.
Nick Robinson was educated at Worth School in Sussex. He went on the study for an English degree at Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge, and then a PGCE in Mathematics at Goldsmith’s College, London University. Nick started his teaching career at Eltham College in south London and after five years returned to Worth Abbey School to become a Housemaster in 1986. He spent 12 years on the staff at Worth as a Housemaster, and also spent one year as a Development Director to lead a successful fundraising campaign for a new Performing Arts Centre. In 1998 Nick was appointed as Headmaster of King’s College Choir School in Cambridge, where he remained for 19 years until his retirement in August 2017. Music has played a central part in Nick’s life. As a teenager he became a conductor of the Sevenoaks Youth Orchestra and while at Eltham College he founded the Eltham College Community Orchestra. He has also sung in various choirs. In November 2004, Nick co-founded a children’s music charity with the Duchess of Kent called ‘Future Talent’, which supports talented children from low-income backgrounds from all parts of the UK up to age 18. Nick has been the Chairman of Future Talent since it was founded and plays a very active part in the life of the charity.
Father Slawomir Witon a native of Poland, is the Dean of Westminster Cathedral, responsible for the whole life of the Cathedral on behalf of the Archbishop. He undertook his priestly formation in London at the Redemptoris Mater House of Formation in Marylebone and at Allen Hall, the Diocesan Seminary, where he read philosophy and theology. As part of his formation he lived and ministered in Kazakhstan and Siberia. Father Witoń was ordained priest in 2005 and was appointed to Westminster Cathedral as a Cathedral Chaplain and subsequently as Sub-Administrator and Master of Ceremonies to the Archbishop, before his appointment as Parish Priest in the busy north London parish of Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Saint George, Enfield, where he ministered for nine years. Father Witoń was appointed Dean of Westminster Cathedral in 2020.
Father Alexander Master was educated at Harrow School and then at Oxford, where he read Literae Humaniores at Corpus Christi College. He was ordained in 2004 and worked in parishes and hospital chaplaincy in Oxford and London before, in 2009, joining the staff of Westminster Cathedral, where he undertook a variety of roles, including Sub-Administrator and Precentor. In 2016 he was appointed Private Secretary to Cardinal Vincent Nichols.
Robert Enserro is a founding partner and the Chief Executive of Macrosynergy, a macroeconomic research and technology company. Robert is responsible for the company’s strategic business development and operations.
From 2005 to 2009, Robert worked at BlueCrest Capital as a Portfolio Manager and Head of Business Development for Emerging Markets. Before joining BlueCrest, Robert was a sovereign debt trader, managing proprietary and flow trading efforts at Deutsche Bank, Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, UBS and Chase Manhattan/Chemical Bank, where he started his professional career.
Prior to working at Deutsche Bank, Robert spent three years at Bank of America, where he created and was Co-Head of the Central Bank Liquidity Desk, the bank’s first cross-product sales effort for central banks and sovereign wealth funds.
Robert graduated with a Bachelor of Science (B.Sc.) in Public Policy and in Spanish from Hamilton College (USA).
Robert and his family moved to London from New York in 2005. He and his wife, Vanessa, have two children. Their son, Francesco, attended WCCS and now attends Westminster School. They are members of Farm Street Church, where both of their children were baptised.
James O’Brien was educated at Prior Park College, Bath, and he read English Literature at the University of Edinburgh. He currently teaches English at Eton and is the House Master in Waynflete. He took up this pastoral role in 2012. James served as Deputy Head of English and Head of E block (Year 10). In addition to his duties at school, James was head coach of Middlesex Schools Under 18 rugby for five years. Before coming to Eton, James taught at Harrow and before that at Downside.
Father Stuart Seaton is the Catholic Chaplain at Harrow School. Father Stuart obtained degrees in Theology from Durham and Leeds Universities prior to being ordained in the Church of England in 1999. He served in parishes and schools as an Anglican minister before being received into the Catholic Church in 2007. He subsequently trained for the Catholic priesthood at Allen Hall Seminary, London, and received dispensation from Pope Benedict XVI to be ordained priest as a married man. Following his ordination in 2010, he became the Catholic Chaplain at Harrow School. In addition to his chaplaincy duties, he teaches Religious Studies and History. He has particular interests in philosophical apologetics, church history and music. He is married to Hilary and they have three sons.
Kate Finch has three children, the youngest of whom, Charlie, was a chorister at WCCS.
Raised in Lancashire, Kate spent her primary years at a state RC school before moving to Bolton School Girls’ Division where she remained for her secondary education. Following A Levels she read English at Queen Mary & Westfield College, University of London. During her undergraduate years Kate worked part time at the National Portrait Gallery and on graduating accepted a permanent role in the NPG’s Exhibitions team. She remained there for a couple of years following which she secured a place on the Mountbatten Internship Programme and moved to New York City for a year where she gained hands on business experience managing a small physiotherapy practice and was awarded a Postgraduate Certificate in International Business. In 2000 Kate moved to Bristol to join her husband and there completed post graduate legal training and qualified as a solicitor (with a specialism in commercial property) in a leading Bristol law firm. She remained in private practice until 2012 at which point she elected to take a break and is now self-employed providing general counsel and company secretarial services to a number of global clients, in such diverse sectors as natural resources, property and wine farming.
Kate enjoys a variety of leisure activities including shooting, music and the Arts, although finds no greater relaxation than devouring a good book.
Maria Strauss is a Partner at the law firm Farrer & Co and specialises in employment law and safeguarding cases for a range of clients. Maria was educated at a girls’ grammar school and then studied law at University before completing her legal training at the College of Law.
Laura Pigorini is the founder, sole partner, and managing director of London School Advice, an educational consulting firm specializing in giving advice to families on all aspects related to school and university education in the UK and the US. What began as a search for the best schools and universities for each of her three children, ended up becoming Laura´s passion and, finally, her profession. Laura´s experience led her to create London School Advice, made up of a team of teaching experts, professionals and former heads to help students achieve their goals through an individual path. Laura has been the Founder and Trustee for the Archangel MLD trust. In addition to this, Laura is also a devoted member of the Catholic church and has volunteered at Wormwood Scrubs prison. Laura is married and has three children. They live in London and have made Pimlico their neighbourhood for the past fifteen years.
WHO IS THE PROPRIETOR OF WESTMINSTER CATHEDRAL CHOIR SCHOOL?

Chorister admissions at 8+
A world-class musical and academic education, with up to 100% off fees
Becoming a chorister from Year 4 to Year 8 offers boys the opportunity to join a world-class choir, and a top independent prep school.
All choristers receive generous scholarships, supplemented by means-tested bursaries where needed, meaning an education at one of the best independent schools in London can be completely free-of-charge.
Boys board at the School during the week, going home to their families from Friday evening at 6.30 pm*, until 9.45 am on Sunday morning.
(*Boys in Years 4 & 5 go home a little earlier on Fridays – either after School at 3.50 pm, or after prep (homework) at 5.00 pm.)
All choristers leave WCCS for leading schools at 13+, normally with music scholarships and awards.
Auditions take place throughout the year, and our process will give you and your family plenty of space to consider whether being a chorister is right for your son. There is no cost, and you will not need to make a final decision until after an offer is made.
1. Join a ‘Being a Chorister’ Zoom session
Every half term, we welcome families who are keen to explore what it means to be a chorister. We take a behind-the-scenes look at the life of a chorister, focussing on what it means to board, and we will teach you a song.
Our next Zoom session is on Wednesday 18th November 2026 at 6.30 pm, and on the following dates thereafter.
Wednesday 27th January 2027 Wednesday 3rd March 2027 Wednesday 28th April 2027 Wednesday 9th June 2027
Register for this Zoom session here.
2. Practice one of our sample songs
Candidates can use our backing track to sing along at home to prepare. There are two options, so boys can pick their favourite.
3. Meet with us for an informal chat
Once you have joined us on Zoom, you and your son can come to WCCS to meet the Master of Music for an informal conversation. Your son can sing one of the songs he’s learned.
4. Go forward for a formal audition
The formal audition is not as scary as it sounds. No preparation is needed!
Boys also do some straightforward assessments in English and maths – sample papers here. They can play a piece on an instrument (although they do not need to be learning an instrument to become a chorister here). You can watch a short video on how auditions work in practice here.
What kind of music does Westminster Cathedral Choir sing?
Westminster Cathedral Choir occupies a unique position at the forefront of English Church Music, and remains the only Catholic Cathedral Choir in the world to sing daily Mass and Vespers.
The Choir draws on the finest music of the last millennium. Performances by composers like Byrd and Tallis, unheard for centuries, earned the Choir its reputation, and still feature today. Gregorian Chant, originating in the ninth century, and the works of Palestrina and Victoria from the Golden Age of Catholic Music, form the backbone of the Choir’s repertoire, but it also sings music from across the centuries, including the work of contemporary composers like Sir James MacMillan.
How do boys become such expert musicians so young?
Boys start with singing technique, sight-reading and music theory. Combined with tuition in two instruments, and playing in orchestras and chamber groups, music becomes part of their daily lives. Practising and performing every day except Saturdays makes boys expert and instinctive musicians.

Admissions at Reception
Primary education begins at 4+ in Reception. Before admission, boys must register with the School. Boys may be registered at any time from birth.
Click here to register online for a day boy place.
Boys join the Pre-Prep in the September after they reach four years of age. There are up to twenty-eight places available.
Registered boys will be invited for assessment, and parents to meet the Head of Pre-Prep and Director of Admissions.
We aim for this to be both friendly and personal for the boys. We are looking for potential rather than attainment and, most importantly, for boys who will thrive and be happy at WCCS.
Parents will be offered either a firm or a waiting list place and feedback will be available on all boys, irrespective of outcome.
Parents accepting a firm offer will be asked for a deposit of £2,000, refundable on their son’s departure from the School.
The School gives priority to boys who have siblings at WCCS, subject to satisfactory assessment.
